checklist.note: Cut 2 removes the only backstop on skipping plan review (no merge-gate equivalent exists for plan-reviewer); Cut 1's PLAN_REJECTED exit discards a plan rejection the merge gate cannot see; the unguarded hole's stated mitigation (report disclosure) does not exist.

implementation_invalidated is a known event with a universal transition from any active state (transitions.py:117-120); count_automatic_rounds is the right existing primitive; retired is a valid decision status with a decision retire verb.

A deliberate, review-voiding act is given a required --reason but no report surface, unlike review authorize (value_report.py:63-68, PR#118), and cli/report.py / engineering/value_report.py are not in scope.
Both cuts, the surfaces, the decision retirement and the test anchors line up with the scope list; attestation .jsonl is exempt from scope coverage (attestation.py:220) so its absence is correct.

findings.summary: Re-keying the skip guard's first arm on count_automatic_rounds (per-change, all epochs) lets a plan that was redeclared and never sent to any reviewer be passed by `review skip`: the change already has automatic plan rounds from its first plan cycle, so the arm never fires. Nothing downstream catches it — verify_attestations only blocks a skipped CODE review without --override (attestation.py:285-290) and derive_independence discloses code review only, so a bare plan skip emits plan_approved and merges silently. The epoch-scoped check the plan removes is today the only guard on that route; the fix needs to distinguish 'new epoch after a rejection' from 'new epoch after plan_redeclared' (e.g. count rounds since the last plan_redeclared) rather than dropping epoch scoping entirely.

The decision to leave the redeclare-wider-scope hole unguarded rests on 'plan redeclare records its reason in redeclaration_history and report renders it', but no report path reads redeclaration_history: it exists only on the derived state (core/reducer.py:157, core/state.py:64) and neither engineering/value_report.py nor cli/report.py references it. The trade the plan makes (no guard, because the route is disclosed) buys nothing, so an implementer following it ships a route that is both unguarded and absent from every accountability surface.

The plan argues the plan_approved+implementation_complete precondition prevents a plan-review bypass, but reopen from PLAN_REJECTED (an explicit test anchor, line 126) discards the rejection itself: the change returns to IMPLEMENTATION_IN_PROGRESS, `done` and code review carry it to READY_TO_MERGE, and verify_attestations is satisfied by the stale plan_approved milestone from the earlier epoch (attestation.py:28,151). The mechanism cannot tell 'the findings were code-level' (the case this change exists for) from 'the reviewer rejected the plan', so PLAN_REJECTED becomes advisory for any change that has implemented once — a distinct hole from the scope-widening one, and stated nowhere.

The plan places reopen in review authorize's consequence class and copies its required --reason, but not the half that makes authorize accountable: value_report.py:63-68 counts authorizations in `report` precisely so a figure can be falsified from memory. implementation_invalidated is rendered by nothing, and cli/report.py / engineering/value_report.py are absent from the scope list, so a verb that voids a passed review leaves no visible trace outside the raw event stream.

checklist.note: Cut 1 and Cut 2 compose into a route that passes never-reviewed code: after `implementation reopen` the new code-review epoch has zero rounds, but Cut 2's new boundary (re-declaration only) still counts the pre-reopen rounds, so the round-evidence guard — today the only mechanical check on that position — no longer fires. The plan enumerates the whole-change variant of this hole but not the one its own Cut 1 creates.

`implementation_invalidated` is already in core/events.py's allowed set and is universal in core/transitions.py; the reopen->done->re-review loop is legal (implementation_complete is not enforced single-fire — .harness/attestations/review-contract-compiler.jsonl carries 12 of them); `retired` is a valid DecisionStatus with a `decision retire` verb. Placing the predicate beside count_automatic_rounds is consistent with review_runs.py's role as the pure fold module.

Scope covers the derived surfaces the change touches (AGENTS.md via the two adapters, docs/cli-reference.md noted as regenerated) and the gate-suggestion tests in tests/unit/gates + daemon hook tests. The retired decision is not `@decision:`-anchored anywhere, so retiring it does not break `decision check`.

The replacement skip predicate is stated only as "rounds frozen since the change was last re-declared" — it never states that it is scoped to the reviewer role, nor whether human-authorized (automatic=false) rounds count, and no test anchor pins either. Both are load-bearing: the current code derives both properties from `execution.rounds`.

findings.summary: Cut 1 + Cut 2 together open a route that passes code no reviewer ever saw. Today the skip guard's first arm keys on the CURRENT epoch, and the code-reviewer epoch boundary is `implementation_complete` (review_runs.py:13). Cut 2 moves that key to `plan_redeclared`/`intent_redeclared` only. So the sequence Cut 1 exists to enable — READY_TO_MERGE -> `implementation reopen` -> edit -> `done` -> `review skip --override --reason` — now passes the guard on rounds frozen BEFORE the reopen, and lands `code_review_passed` on an implementation that was never sent to a code reviewer. `verify_attestations` does not catch it (engineering/attestation.py:283-287 blocks only a skipped code review lacking `--override`), so it merges as pass-with-disclosure. The plan reasons explicitly about the whole-change variant of exactly this hole ("a change re-declared with a wider scope and never sent to any reviewer") and rejects it for that reason, but does not notice that `implementation reopen` re-creates the same position without a re-declaration. The boundary needs to include the role's own reset event (`implementation_invalidated` / `implementation_complete` for code-reviewer), not re-declaration alone.

The new predicate is specified as "rounds frozen since the change was last re-declared" and never says it is scoped to the reviewer role. The code it replaces gets that scoping for free: `derive_review_execution` filters `payload['reviewer'] != reviewer`, so `execution.rounds` is per-role. A predicate written over the raw event stream without the reviewer filter — which is what the plan's prose describes — lets plan-review rounds satisfy the guard for `review skip --reviewer code-reviewer`, i.e. skipping code review on a change where no code-review round was ever frozen. That is the guard's original purpose, and the only test anchor covering it ("a change with no round ever frozen is still refused") passes under both readings, so nothing turns red. Two implementers will build different predicates here; state the reviewer filter and add an anchor for "plan rounds present, zero code-reviewer rounds -> code-reviewer skip still refused".

The plan does not say whether the new predicate counts human-authorized rounds. It directs the predicate to sit "beside `count_automatic_rounds`", whose body filters `payload.get('automatic', True)`; an implementer who mirrors that neighbour excludes authorized rounds. The code being replaced does not: `execution.rounds` carries both automatic and authorized rounds. Under the filtered reading, a change whose only rounds since re-declaration were human-authorized — which is precisely the state a change reaches after the round budget fires, and precisely when a wedged producer needs the escape hatch — can no longer be skipped. Say "every frozen round, automatic or authorized" (or the opposite, deliberately) so the choice is not inherited from the neighbouring function's signature.

checklist.note: The per-role reset table adopted in this delta rests on a premise the code contradicts: `plan_ready` is not merely a re-submission of the same plan. `plan ready --scope` is legal from PLAN_REJECTED (core/transitions.py:38) and the reducer replaces cs.scope outright (core/reducer.py:141-144), so a rejected change can widen its scope arbitrarily without any redeclaration and then satisfy the repaired guard on rounds frozen against the old, narrower plan — the same silent-merge route the delta itself rejects draft-1 for.

Placing the new fold in engineering/review_runs.py beside count_automatic_rounds, keying on review_round_started, and keeping the budget fold separate all fit the existing event-fold design. The code-reviewer row is sound: implementation_complete is not re-emitted on the CODE_REVIEW_REJECTED loop (transitions.py:46-48), but Cut 1's reopen → done does re-emit it, so the reset lands exactly where the delta claims and Cut 1 cannot walk code past the guard.

Asymmetry with the PR#98 budget fold is stated and pinned by a test anchor; the 'retired' status named for the decision doc is in the ratified vocabulary (core/decisions.py:20-21); the IndexError trap in the second arm is called out rather than left to the implementer.

The added anchors cover each claim the delta makes that is checkable — the Cut1/Cut2 cross-check, the role filter, the authorized-round case, and the empty-current-epoch IndexError. Note the anchor set will need one more case once the architecture finding is resolved.

findings.summary: The plan-reviewer reset boundary (`plan_redeclared`/`intent_redeclared`, explicitly **not** `plan_ready`) is justified by the claim that "a `plan_ready` after a rejection is the same plan revised". That is not true of scope. `("PLAN_REJECTED", "plan_ready")` is a legal transition (core/transitions.py:38), `plan ready` accepts `--scope` from that state (cli/plan.py:185-226), and the reducer ALWAYS replaces `cs.scope` from the latest plan_ready rather than merging (core/reducer.py:141-144). So: reject → `plan ready <c> --scope @wider` → AWAITING_PLAN_REVIEW → `review skip --reviewer plan-reviewer` passes, because rounds frozen against the OLD narrower plan still sit after the last re-declaration. That emits `plan_approved` for a scope no reviewer ever saw, and by the delta's own analysis nothing downstream catches it — verify_attestations blocks only a skipped *code* review lacking --override (engineering/attestation.py:283-287) and derive_independence discloses code review alone, so it merges silently. This is the identical failure the delta rejects the whole-change draft for, reached by a cheaper route that needs no redeclaration at all. The rule stated at the top of the section ("resets when there is genuinely new material for that role") is the right rule; the plan-reviewer row does not implement it, because a scope-replacing plan_ready IS new material. Either add a scope-changing `plan_ready` to the plan-reviewer reset set (e.g. reset when the emitted `scope` differs from the prior one, which is derivable from the same raw stream the predicate already walks), or state and close the gap another way — but as written an implementer following the table ships the hole.

findings.summary: The new Out-of-scope paragraph defers plan-skip invisibility as pre-existing, but Cut 2 is what makes the route reachable, and Cut 1's PLAN_REJECTED exclusion is justified by a disclosure that this paragraph shows does not exist. Today `_guard_skip_round_evidence_or_exit` refuses a plan-reviewer skip after a rejection, because `plan_ready` resets the epoch — so reject -> `plan ready` -> `review skip --reviewer plan-reviewer --override` is currently blocked. After Cut 2 that sequence passes on rounds frozen before the rejection, emits `plan_approved`, and `verify_attestations` (attestation.py:283-287) checks only `independence["code_review"]`, so it merges with nothing said at the gate. That makes plan rejection escapable at zero gate-visible cost for any change willing to run one command — the architecture test's silent-wrong-value case. It also breaks the load-bearing sentence at lines 72-75, which excludes PLAN_REJECTED from `implementation reopen` on the grounds that Cut 2's skip 'stamps skipped: true, and is therefore visible to `report` and the merge attestation'; the merge-attestation half is false for this role. Resolve one of two ways: extend the merge-gate disclosure to plan-reviewer inside this change (which makes F3's rationale true and is what the paragraph currently defers), or re-base F3's rationale on the surface that is actually load-bearing and state plainly that the escape is disclosed only in `report`. As written an implementer ships the escape hatch and the deferral together, and the merge boundary loses a signal the plan claims it has.

The rewritten count line claims an outcome the derivation does not measure, contradicting its own comment. The comment immediately above states "Whether the change was reviewed again afterwards is the merge gate's question, not this line's, and claiming it here would assert more than the derivation measured" — yet the line now says each reopen is "sending the change back through code review". The derivation only counts `implementation_invalidated` events; a change reopened and then abandoned or archived never goes back through review, so the count still renders that assertion. The old wording described a past fact the events did carry; the new one describes a future the events do not.
